q.intro.text: A game screen is a coordinate grid. The tip of a sprite is at A: negative two, three.

q.move.text: The game slides the whole sprite five right and four down.

q.ask.text: Where does the tip land? We call that point A prime.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: The whole sprite slides five right and four down. Every point makes the same move: nothing turns or stretches.

e.s2.text: A goes five right, so x changes: negative two plus five is three. Then four down, so y changes: three minus four is negative one. A prime is three, negative one.

e.s3.text: The same move for B and C: add five to x, and subtract four from y. B prime is six, zero: it lands on the x-axis.

e.s4.text: One rule for every point: x, y goes to x plus five, y minus four. Right and left change x. Up and down change y.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does five right change only x?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Right and left are across, along the x-axis. The point stays at the same height, so y does not change.

e.w-both.text: Look at A going right: it stays on the same horizontal line, at height three. Only x changes.

e.w-pos.text: Not always: a point at negative seven that moves five right lands at negative two, still negative. Right adds to x.

t.intro.text: A designer mirrors half of a logo across the y-axis. The first two steps are done for you.

t.s1.text: Fold the grid along the y-axis: the logo flips onto the other side.

t.s2.text: D is five left of the y-axis, so D prime is five right of it: five, one. The fold moves D straight across, so y stays one.

t.ask.text: Your step: F is at negative three, negative two. Where is F prime?

t.f-ok.text: Yes: F is three left of the axis, so F prime is three right of it, at three, negative two. Its y stays negative two.

t.f-named.text: That changes y. A fold across the y-axis moves F sideways, so x changes, and y stays negative two.

t.f-both.text: Only one coordinate changes. A sideways fold keeps the height: y stays negative two.

t.f-same.text: F prime is on the other side of the axis. The opposite of negative three is three, a positive number.

t.f-other.text: Count from the y-axis: F is three left of it. F prime is three right of it, at the same height.

t.rule.text: Now write the rule for every point: tap the new x, then the new y.

t.r-ok.text: Yes: x, y goes to negative x, y. Across the y-axis, x becomes its opposite, and y stays.

t.r-named.text: That is the rule for the x-axis. This fold moves points sideways, so x is the one that changes.

t.r-both.text: Changing both signs would turn the logo upside down too. Only x changes.

t.r-same.text: Then nothing would move. The fold sends x to its opposite.

t.r-slot.text: The first box is the new x, the second box is the new y.

t.cb-0.text: At the start you picked three, negative one. Right: left and right change x, up and down change y. A sideways fold changes x too.

t.cb-1.text: At the start you picked negative six, eight: the move to the right went into y. Left and right change x only, the same idea as this fold.

t.cb-2.text: At the start you picked negative seven, negative one. Negative two plus five is three: start at negative two and go five to the right.

t.cb-sure.text: And you were certain. Worth remembering: check which way the point moves before you change a number.

p.intro.text: Jordan reflects K, four, negative three, across the x-axis, and writes K prime, negative four, negative three. It's the x-axis, so x changes sign.

p.build-no.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build-yes.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.k1.text: A fold across the x-axis moves K straight up or down,

p.k2.text: so K prime keeps the x-coordinate four,

p.k3.text: and K prime is three above the axis: four, three.

p.c1.text: The fold line from K is vertical: it meets the x-axis at a right angle.

p.c2.text: K and K prime sit on the same vertical line, x equals four.

p.c3.text: Three below, three above. Jordan's point is a fold across the y-axis instead.

p.w-named.text: That's Jordan's slip. The axis names the mirror, not the coordinate that changes.

p.w-both.text: Changing both signs is a half turn around the origin, not a fold.

p.w-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof: a fold across the x-axis moves points up or down, so x stays, and y becomes its opposite: x, y goes to x, negative y.
